title: Complexity of directed detours
formal: Classify the worst-case complexity of the following decision problem on unrestricted finite directed graphs: given distinct vertices s and t, is there a simple directed s-to-t path with at least \(\operatorname{dist}_{G}(s,t)+1\) edges? The requested distinction is polynomial-time solvability versus NP-completeness. This is the fixed \(k=1\) case of Longest Detour, not the problem with k supplied as part of the input.
context:
The question asks for strictly greater length. A graph may have many different shortest s-to-t paths and still have no simple path longer than them. Finding a second distinct path therefore does not by itself decide the problem.

Allowing a walk to revisit a cycle would make it possible to add length without producing the required simple path. The distinct-vertex condition is essential to this complexity question.

Shortest paths are efficiently computable, but deciding whether their length can be exceeded by a simple path constrains which vertices can be reused. Here even one additional edge is the unresolved threshold.

The source gives a fixed-parameter algorithm for planar digraphs, and the 2023 follow-up gives an \(O(n^{2})\) algorithm for this \(k=1\) case. These results do not apply to arbitrary digraphs.

Longest Path Above Diameter asks for a path exceeding the graph’s diameter, rather than the distance between prescribed endpoints. Its \(k=1\) hardness theorem does not classify Directed Detour.
why: Pinpoints whether even the smallest departure from shortest-path length creates NP-complete difficulty under the simple-path constraint, a basic boundary in directed path algorithms.
status_note: Read the complete original target and the JCSS 2023 conclusion, and checked the planar follow-up. Exact-target searches through 12 September 2026 found no classification for arbitrary digraphs. A July 2026 second-shortest-simple-path abstract was also inspected, but did not establish a result for the strictly-longer-than-all-shortest-paths predicate here.

definitions: The input is a directed graph \(G=(V,E)\), with \(V=[n], n\ge 2\), no loops or parallel arcs, and distinguished \(s\ne t\). Both opposite arcs between two vertices are allowed. The graph is unweighted; every arc has length one. A simple s-to-t path is a sequence \(v_{0}=s,v_{1},\ldots ,v_{\ell}=t\) of pairwise distinct vertices with \((v_{j- 1},v_{j})\in E\) for \(1\le j\le \ell\), and its length is \(\ell\). If t is reachable from \(s, \operatorname{dist}_{G}(s,t)\) is the minimum length of such a path. If t is unreachable, the instance is a no-instance. The input lists all vertices and arcs using binary vertex labels; N is the full encoding length. Polynomial time means one deterministic multitape Turing machine that decides every instance in at most \(C(N+1)^{a}\) steps for absolute constants C,a. NP-completeness uses deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions; in particular, a hardness proof can give a map from Boolean satisfiability instances to these graph instances that preserves yes/no answers. The decision problem is in NP: an at-most-n-vertex path is a polynomial-size certificate, and reachability distance and the path conditions can be checked in polynomial time. No planarity, acyclicity, connectivity or uniqueness of shortest paths is promised.
answer_criterion: Determine the problem’s complexity in the stated unrestricted directed, unweighted model. A deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm establishes tractability; a polynomial-time many-one reduction from SAT establishes NP-completeness, since membership in NP is known. The latter excludes a polynomial-time algorithm under \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). The question does not assume a \(\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{NP}\)-complete dichotomy in advance; any different established classification must explain the remaining boundary. Bounds only for planar graphs, or hardness when k is variable, do not classify the fixed \(k=1\) problem.
